[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"DataParallel vs. DistributedDataParallel (DDP) in PyTorch"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Scaling deep learning models across multiple GPUs is essential for handling large datasets and complex architectures. PyTorch offers two primary paradigms for data-parallel training: DataParallel (DP) and DistributedDataParallel (DDP). Understanding their architectural differences is critical for optimizing training performance."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Overview of DataParallel (DP)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"DataParallel is designed to be a single-process, multi-thread paradigm. It wraps your PyTorch module, splits the batch along the batch dimension, distributes the data to each GPU, and gathers the output back to the primary GPU."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Extremely easy to implement, requiring only a single line of code changes to wrap the model."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Suffers from the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) bottleneck, heavily relies on a single master GPU for gradient aggregation, and incurs high overhead due to scattering and gathering tensors."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Overview of DistributedDataParallel (DDP)"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"DistributedDataParallel uses a multi-process paradigm. It spawns a separate training process for each GPU, even across multiple machines. Each process handles its own optimizer step and synchronizes gradients using ring-allreduce communication via the torch.distributed backend."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: No GIL contention, scales efficiently across multiple GPUs and nodes, and drastically reduces communication overhead."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Requires proper initialization of the process group and careful management of data loaders."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Code Example: Implementing DataParallel (DP)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The following snippet demonstrates how to set up DataParallel in a standard PyTorch training loop."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = MyModel()
if torch.cuda.device_count() > 1:
    print(f"Let's use {torch.cuda.device_count()} GPUs!")
    model = nn.DataParallel(model)

model = model.to('cuda')"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Code Example: Implementing DistributedDataParallel (DDP)"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"To implement DDP, you must initialize the process group, wrap your model with DDP, and use DistributedSampler for your DataLoader."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data.distributed import DistributedSampler

# Initialize the process group
dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
rank = dist.get_rank()

# Setup model and move to specific GPU
model = MyModel().to(rank)
model = DDP(model, device_ids=[rank])

# Setup dataset sampler
sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset)
data_loader = DataLoader(dataset, sampler=sampler, batch_size=32)"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary Recommendation"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"While DataParallel is simpler to setup for quick experiments on a single machine, PyTorch officially recommends DistributedDataParallel for all multi-GPU training scenarios due to its superior speed, scalability, and modern multi-process architecture."}]
